summary: This document provides a set of public key cryptography test keys, for use where pre-generated keys and operations like digital signatures are needed. Like the EICAR and GTUBE test files, these publicly known keys can be recognized by applications as test-only and are given no security properties.

plainLanguage.summary: Everyone knows the code to this practice lock, so nobody should trust it for anything real. It is great for testing, and software can spot it as pretend.

questions: test keys for public key cryptography
subtitle: Well-known, publicly available cryptographic keys for testing, analogous to EICAR and GTUBE test files.

tldr.problem: Many applications use preconfigured or sample cryptographic keys for testing, but no standard set exists. This leads to security risks when test keys ship in production code, and different applications use different, undocumented keys, making it hard to recognize test data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9500 provides a standardized set of publicly known test keys across three major algorithm families: RSA (1024, 2048, 4096 bits), discrete logarithm algorithms (DSA, Diffie-Hellman, ElGamal), and elliptic curve algorithms (ECDSA, ECDH) in various sizes. The keys are published both in C-like source code notation (for direct use in crypto code) and in OpenSSL private key format (for standard tools).
tldr.outcome: Applications can now use standard, widely recognized test keys. Like the EICAR antivirus test file and GTUBE spam test file, these keys are immediately recognizable to software as being for testing only, with no security properties, reducing the risk of test keys reaching production.

facts.value: C source code and OpenSSL PEM format

today: RFC 9500 is an Informational RFC from the IETF, published in December 2023. It represents IETF consensus and is not on the standards track. It provides the first standard set of test keys for public key cryptography; future algorithm families should update this RFC while maintaining compatibility with the format and naming conventions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Public key cryptography is fundamental to secure communication and authentication on the Internet, but developing and testing cryptographic code is complex. Testing requires pre-generated keys, and applications often use sample or preconfigured keys during development. However, these test keys are often undocumented, inconsistent across projects, and risk being accidentally deployed to production.

This RFC provides standardized test keys analogous to the EICAR test file (used by antivirus software) and the GTUBE test file (used by spam filters). These test files are non-malicious, publicly known, and recognized by security software as being purely for testing. Similarly, the test keys in this RFC are publicly known and can be recognized by applications as test-only, with no security properties assigned.

The keys cover three major algorithm families commonly used in production systems: RSA, algorithms based on the Discrete Logarithm Problem (DLP) like DSA and Diffie-Hellman, and algorithms based on the Elliptic Curve Discrete Logarithm Problem (ECDLP) like ECDSA and ECDH. Although some algorithms and key sizes are no longer recommended (such as RSA-1024), they are included to accommodate large installed bases of legacy systems.
sections.plainLanguage: For testing antivirus, there's a harmless file everyone recognizes as a test. For testing crypto software, there are now standard keys that everyone can spot as test keys.

sections.title: Test Key Organization and Formats
sections.content:
The RFC provides test keys in two formats: C-like source code notation for direct inclusion in code, and OpenSSL private key format for use with standard cryptographic tools.

In the source code format, each key element is represented as a bit count followed by a byte array in big-endian form. For example, an RSA key includes components for the modulus (n), public exponent (e), private exponent (d), first prime factor (p), second prime factor (q), and CRT coefficients. Each element is given a recommended variable name for use in source code as a standard reference.

The OpenSSL format representation allows the same keys to be used with standard utilities like OpenSSL directly, without manual parsing. This dual presentation enables testing in both custom cryptographic code (using the source form) and with standard tools (using the OpenSSL form).
sections.plainLanguage: The test keys are printed in two ways: as data you can copy into your code, or in a standard format that existing tools already understand.

sections.title: RSA, DLP, and ECDLP Key Sets
sections.content:
RSA keys are provided in sizes 1024, 2048, and 4096 bits. The 1024-bit key is below modern recommendations but is included for testing systems that still use it. Each RSA key includes the public modulus, public and private exponents, prime factors, and CRT optimization coefficients.

DLP-based keys (for algorithms like DSA, Diffie-Hellman, and ElGamal) are provided at various key sizes. These algorithms rely on the difficulty of computing discrete logarithms in a finite field or group. DLP keys include parameters like the prime modulus, generator, and private/public key values.

ECDLP-based keys (for algorithms like ECDSA and ECDH) are provided for common curves such as NIST P-256, P-384, P-521, secp256k1, and others. Each ECDLP key is specific to its curve and includes the curve parameters and the key's private/public point values.

The RFC explicitly notes that it does not attempt to cover every possible algorithm family, as new ones constantly appear and disappear. If future algorithm families require test keys, similar documents should update this RFC and maintain compatibility with the format and naming conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: RSA keys come in small, medium, and large. DLP keys work with field math. ECDLP keys work with curves. The RFC covers the big families and is designed to be extended later if new methods emerge.

sections.title: Key Encoding and Naming Conventions
sections.content:
Each test key is given a recommended name for use in source code following a consistent pattern. RSA keys are named like testRSA1024, testRSA2048, and testRSA4096. DLP and ECDLP keys follow similar naming patterns based on their algorithm and size.

The bit count in each key component specifies the nominal key size. Key components are encoded as byte arrays in big-endian (most significant byte first) format. For example, in an RSA key where the modulus is 1024 bits, the byte array contains 128 bytes (1024 bits / 8 bits per byte).

The naming conventions and source code format are designed to be easily incorporated into cryptographic code in languages like C, C++, Java, JavaScript, Go, Swift, and Rust, covering the majority of languages likely to be used for crypto implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each test key has a simple name like 'testRSA2048'. Numbers in the key are stored as bytes, biggest part first, ready to drop into code.

sections.title: Use Cases and Security Implications
sections.content:
The intended use of these test keys is anywhere a preconfigured or sample key is required: unit testing of cryptographic code, testing of signature or key agreement implementations, testing of certificate chains, and any similar scenario where real cryptographic keys would not be appropriate but test keys are needed.

Because these keys are publicly known, they provide zero security. Applications and developers must ensure that test keys never reach production systems. Tools can be configured to detect and reject these well-known test keys, similar to how antivirus software detects and whitelists the EICAR test file.

The presence of these standard test keys allows developers to write portable, reproducible tests that work across different implementations and platforms. Since the keys are the same everywhere, test vectors and expected signatures can be shared and verified across projects.
sections.plainLanguage: Use these keys for testing code, testing signatures, and testing certificate chains—anything involving crypto that isn't for production. Software can recognize them as harmless test keys. Never ship them in production code.
